name: Kierki
description: Kierki (Polish Hearts) is the Polish variant of the classic avoidance trick-taking game Hearts. Played by four players, it features a unique multi-hand structure where the objective changes each roundâ€”from avoiding hearts to avoiding queens, or taking no tricks at all. It is a game of high strategic depth and defensive maneuvering.

history.origins: Derived from the pan-European 'Hearts' family (like Black Lady in the US and Gong Zhu in China), Kierki was standardized in Poland in the late 20th century.
timeline: Mid-1900s: Hearts variants circulate in Eastern Europe.
1970s: The characteristic 7-hand 'Series' structure of Kierki becomes standard.
Present: One of Poland's most popular social card games; widely available on Polish gaming portals.
history.cultural: In Poland, the term 'Kierki' (meaning Hearts) is synonymous with tactical defensive play.
history.evolution: The game evolved to include several 'Penalty Hands' before the final 'Positive Hand', creating a long-form competitive format.

setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Aces are high, 2s are low.

rules.objective: Avoid taking specific penalty cards or tricks across a series of rounds.
rules.gameplay:
1. Standard trick-taking. Must follow suit.
2. No trumps are used in most Kierki variants.
3. The leading player can lead any card (except Hearts in the first trick of the Hearts hand).
keyRules: Must follow suit if able; otherwise may play any card.
In hearts-related hands (no hearts, no king of hearts, bandit), must not lead a heart unless void in other suits.
Trick is won by the highest card of the suit led; no trumps in the first seven deals.
Dealer deals all 52 cards one at a time, 13 to each player; turn to deal passes left after each hand.
Player to dealer's left leads to the first trick; winner of each trick leads to the next.

strategy.basic: Keep track of the Queens and the King of Hearts. If you hold the King of Hearts, you must try to 'void' yourself in another suit so you can dump the King as soon as someone leads Hearts.
strategy.intermediate: Ducking the 7th Trick: In Hand 6, count the tricks! If you are on trick 6 and you have a high card, play it now to avoid being forced to win trick 7.
strategy.advanced: The 'Reverse Void': In the Positive Hands (8-11), your objective flips. Try to trick your opponents into winning the low-value tricks so you can secure your bid.
tips: In the Master Hand (Hand 7), avoid taking ANY tricks. It is far better to draw twice than to risk taking a trick containing a Queen and the King of Hearts.
High cards are liabilities in the first 7 hands but assets in the last 4â€”adjust your valuation accordingly.
